The Incomplete Story of Nanoplastics

Good morning, everyone! Thanks for being here. As we wrap up our time together for the semester, I hope you’ve taken away something new. Even after just a handful of meetings, you are probably in the top fraction of a percent of people who know anything substantial about microplastics and nanoplastics.

When we did the demonstration with the plastic-lined cup earlier this week, we touched on a very real public anxiety. People are worried about plastic exposures because there are so many unknowns. If there is one overarching message I hope you take away from our discussions on release, exposure, and hazard, it is this: the story is really incomplete.

Right now, in terms of both research and policy, we aren’t sure what to say. Is it safe to ingest the amount of plastic that we do? Or is there serious harm associated with it? It is a challenging space to navigate. On one hand, it is a silver lining for those of you interested in research—there is immense opportunity here. On the other hand, there could be real health outcomes that people are experiencing right now.

Let’s recall our discussion from Wednesday about single-use beverage cups. We looked at a study demonstrating that when these cups come into contact with water—hot or cold—they release nanoscale particles.

But notice what that study did not measure. It didn’t tell us whether anyone who uses those cups and ingests the particles actually absorbs them into their human tissue. It also didn’t tell us if there are any adverse health effects.

So, how is measuring particle release different from measuring health risk?

Exposure, Hazard, and Risk: Defining Our Terms

To understand health impacts, we need to break the problem down into a simple conceptual model.

First, we have exposure. This simply means contact. How are we exposed, and how much? We often think of ingestion—drinking or eating. But what about inhalation? A colleague of mine in civil engineering who studies aerosol chemistry (and became quite well-known during the pandemic for her work on airborne droplets) pointed out that microplastics research is heavily skewed toward drinking water.

Think about it: how much drinking water do you ingest a day? Probably about one to two liters. Now, how many liters of air do you breathe every day? Thousands. Thousands of liters of air are going in and out of your lungs daily. I can guarantee that right now, there are microplastics floating around in this room, shedding off our clothing and carpets. So, exposure is multifaceted.

Next is hazard. Does the material we are exposed to have the capacity to cause harm? There are seven main categories of plastics, but within those, there are thousands of chemical variations to tweak colors or flexibility. All of this chemistry dictates whether a particle presents a hazard.

Finally, we have risk. If we know the exposure and we know the hazard, what is the actual likelihood and severity of harm under those specific conditions? The cup study only demonstrated release; it left massive gaps in our understanding of exposure and hazard, meaning we couldn’t even begin to calculate risk.

If a new study proves that a specific plastic chemical is highly toxic to human cells in a petri dish, have the researchers established the health risk of that plastic?

Not quite! They have only established the hazard—the capacity of that chemical to cause harm. To figure out the actual risk, we would also need to know the exposure, meaning how much of that plastic people actually come into contact with in their daily lives.

Study 1: The Proof of Ingestion

Today, we are going to talk about poop—at least in part. We are going to look at a very short paper from the Annals of Internal Medicine that investigated microplastics in human stool.

The background is straightforward: microplastics are ubiquitous in our environment and have been found in the plants and animals we eat. They are in the food chain. The researchers wanted to know: if we take a sampling of people, what will we find exiting their bodies? They looked at eight participants from different countries in Europe and Asia.

To analyze the samples, they used a sieve—much like a window screen—to retain any particles larger than 50 micrometers. Let’s look at what they found.

In the top left of the figure, we see a light microscope image of a particle. The scale bar is 500 micrometers, which is roughly ten times the width of a human hair. Next to it is a fluorescence image. This technique uses infrared light—which our eyes cannot see—to look for chemical correlations.

Accuracy Note

Possible error: Fluorescence microscopy does not use infrared light to identify materials by chemical correlation. The technique shown and described is infrared (FTIR) microspectroscopy, which measures vibrational absorption of infrared radiation.

Correction: The image is an infrared (or FTIR) chemical map, a technique that uses infrared absorption to identify the chemical composition of the particle.

The graph at the bottom is a spectrogram. The x-axis shows the wave number (similar to wavelength) and the y-axis shows transmission. Notice the dips in the graph? Those are absorption features. By comparing the spectrum of the unknown microparticle (the solid line) to a known reference spectrum for polyethylene terephthalate, or PET (the dotted line), we can see how closely the features line up. It acts just like a chemical fingerprint. This strong correlation tells us the particle is indeed PET plastic, which we certainly wouldn’t expect to find in human stool naturally.

The results were striking: all eight participants excreted plastics. The median was 20 particles per 10 grams of stool, mostly consisting of polypropylene and PET.

However, any good scientific paper will point out its own limitations. This was a very narrow sample set—only eight people, and only one sample per person. Furthermore, they only measured particles down to 50 micrometers. Nanoplastics were entirely ignored, frankly due to the analytical challenges of measuring things that small. We also don’t know the source of the plastic. Was it from food, toothpaste, or chewing gum?

Most importantly, what does detection in stool actually mean?

When we ingest particles, they enter our gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Our bodies have evolved to extract the nutrients and hydration we need while shielding us from harmful substances. If a particle remains within the gut and is excreted, the body has effectively protected us.

The other possibility is uptake. Some particles might cross the intestinal barriers and enter our tissues or bloodstream. The extent of this uptake depends on the particle’s size, chemistry, and other conditions.

So, finding plastics in stool proves that ingestion occurred, and it proves that the body is getting rid of at least some of it. But it does not prove systemic absorption. We don’t know if any particles were retained in the body, and we don’t even know the initial dose that went in. Therefore, we cannot use this study to draw conclusions about health risks.

If a patient has a high count of microplastics in their stool sample, does that mean their internal organs are heavily contaminated with plastic?

We actually can’t make that leap! Finding plastics in stool just tells us the gastrointestinal tract did its job by acting as a barrier and excreting the particles. It doesn’t tell us whether any of those particles crossed the gut wall to enter the bloodstream or internal tissues.

Study 2: Exploring Hazard in the Lab

Since the stool study couldn’t tell us about tissue uptake, let’s look at a second study that tries to model that exact interaction. This paper, published in Science of the Total Environment, looks at the accumulation of nanoplastics in human intestinal organoids.

What is an organoid? In the laboratory, scientists can take human-derived cells (like stem cells) and grow them into three-dimensional structures that closely replicate parts of our internal organs. In this case, they grew an organoid that mimics the layered structure of the human small intestine.

The researchers exposed these organoids to nanoplastics. If you look at the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images in the figure, you’ll see the particles they used. They are roughly 50 nanometers in size. Notice their shape? They are flawless, uniform spheres made of polystyrene.

Do you think the nanoplastics we ingest in the real world look like ideal spheres? Definitely not. Real-world plastics are irregular, jagged fragments of varying sizes and chemistries. This is a very simplified, idealized model.

Why might an experiment using flawless, 50-nanometer polystyrene spheres fail to predict how our bodies react to a degraded plastic water bottle?

Real-world plastics break down into jagged, irregular fragments of all different sizes and chemical makeups. While uniform spheres are great for controlled lab experiments, they don’t capture the messy reality of the shapes and chemistries we actually ingest.

Over a two-day period, the researchers observed that these polystyrene particles associated with and accumulated in the intestinal cells. After two weeks, they looked for cellular responses and found two main outcomes: apoptosis (which is a type of controlled cell death) and inflammation (which is often associated with disease).

This study gives us a glimpse into hazard. We see an exposure leading to a negative biological response. But we must remember the context: organoids are just models. They do not have a full circulatory system with flowing blood, complex pH gradients, or other competing molecules. Exposing a lab-grown tissue to a high dose of uniform polystyrene spheres is very different from a human drinking out of a plastic-lined cup.

Bridging the Gap: What We Still Need to Know

We keep coming back to our foundational concept:

The equation \text{Risk} = \text{Hazard} \times \text{Exposure} is a helpful conceptual shorthand, but it is a far cry from a complete, quantitative risk model.

If we look at the claims we can confidently make based on the evidence we’ve reviewed:

  • Can plastic-lined cups release nanoparticles into water? Supported.

  • Have microplastics been detected in human stool? Supported.

  • Do all ingested nanoplastics cross the gut wall? Not established.

  • Can 50 nm polystyrene cause cellular responses in organoids? Supported.

  • Is the human health risk of a typical beverage cup known precisely? Not established.

So, how do we move forward? What evidence would actually close these gaps?

To truly understand the risk, the scientific community needs to answer several complex questions:

  • Exposure: How much plastic are we actually ingesting or inhaling at realistic, everyday concentrations?

  • Internal Dose: What fraction of that plastic remains in the gut and is excreted, versus the fraction that successfully crosses barriers and enters our tissues?

  • Hazard: Which specific biological effects occur at these realistic doses and sizes? (Remember, lab experiments often use artificially high doses just to ensure they can measure a response).

  • Risk: Do these realistic human exposures actually cause measurable, adverse health outcomes in the general population?

When we make scientific claims, they must match the evidence. Detection does not equal absorption. Just because a particle is present doesn’t mean it is crossing our biological barriers. Similarly, demonstrating a possible hazard in a controlled lab setting does not automatically establish a real-world risk at everyday doses.

There is a tremendous amount of uncertainty right now. We cannot definitively say that everything is safe, nor can we say that everything is harmful. Chances are, the reality lies somewhere in between. And that is exactly why this field of research is so exciting and so necessary.
